Mrs Kristie Maggar v Laura Brown

28 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4197Employment & workplace
LN Veterinary sought costs after Ms Maggar discontinued her unfair dismissal application. The Fair Work Commission refused costs under s 611(2), but ordered $980.75 under s 400A for unreasonable procedural conduct concerning a late adjournment request and failure to instruct her lawyer. The decision is [2026] FWC 4197 (Commissioner McKinnon, 28 October 2026).
Key holding

Under s 400A, costs may be ordered where a party’s unreasonable act or omission in connection with the conduct or continuation of the matter caused the other party to incur costs.

The FWC may make an order for costs against a party to a matter arising under this Part (the first party) for costs incurred by the other party to the matter if the FWC is satisfied that the first party caused those costs to be incurred because of an unreasonable act or omission of the first party in connection with the conduct or continuation of the matter.

Danielle Leonard v Cadence Talent Pty Ltd

28 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4161Employment & workplace
Danielle Leonard lodged a s 365 general protections application alleging dismissal in contravention of Part 3-1 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The application was filed out of time after an earlier unfair dismissal application was discontinued, and the Commission refused an extension of time and dismissed the application.
Key holding

An extension of time under s 366 requires the Commission to be satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist, assessed against the s 366(2) considerations.

The Commission can extend time only if it is satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances. On balance, the considerations above do not weigh in favour of exceptional circumstances in support of an extension of time.

United Firefighters' Union of Australia (259V) v Triple Zero Victoria

28 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4199Employment & workplace
The UFU applied under s.739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Commission to determine whether a TZV employee was entitled to an independent investigator for serious misconduct allegations. The Commission held that neither the Triple Zero Victoria Operations Enterprise Agreement 2024 nor the TZV Workplace Investigations Procedure created that entitlement. It nonetheless recommended that Mr Walker proceed as TZV’s appointed investigator.
Key holding

Clause 67.4 requires any summary dismissal to be carried out in accordance with TZV policies and procedures consistent with the FW Act and Regulations, but it does not incorporate those policies into the Agreement or create a pre-dismissal entitlement to an independent investigation.

Properly construed, in my view, what the clause commits the Respondent to do is to enact the "summary dismissal of any employee" in accordance with its policies and procedures which must be consistent with the provisions of the Act and FW Regulations.

CFMEU (105N) v Flinders Adelaide Container Terminal Pty Ltd Trading AS Flinders Adelaide Container Terminal

28 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4200Employment & workplace
The FWC determined a dispute under the Flinders Adelaide Container Terminal Stevedoring Enterprise Agreement 2021–2025 about whether Mr Conway was entitled to permanent reclassification from Grade 3 to Grade 5. It held the 70% higher-duty threshold is a gateway only, not a mandatory entitlement, and that FACT’s refusal was consistent with the Agreement because it applied permissible merit/conduct considerations under cl 26.5.4.
Key holding

Meeting the 70% higher-duty threshold under cl 26.5.3 only permits an application and does not entitle an employee to permanent reclassification; once the gateway is met, the employer may refuse on merit principles relating to the employee’s performance, attendance, conduct or attitude.

once an employee meets the threshold of having worked seventy per cent of shifts for which they are available at a higher grade over the previous twelve months they can apply for a permanent r eclassification. Once the employee submits their application in accordance with the provisions of clause 26.5.1 and 26.5.2, the Respondent can apply merit principles as they relate to the performance or conduct of the employee to determine if the reclassification will be granted.

Prabhatkumar Valabhai Zala v Shred-X Pty Ltd

28 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4204Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission dismissed Mr Zala’s s.394 unfair dismissal application after Shred-X objected that he was not dismissed. Mr Zala resigned after a manager’s inappropriate comment and a period of psychological injury, but the Commission found Shred-X did not force him to resign. The application was dismissed for want of jurisdiction under s.386 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).
Key holding

Whether a resignation was forced is assessed objectively by reference to the employer’s conduct, not the employee’s subjective feeling.

It is the conduct of the employer that must be assessed, not whether the employee subjectively felt like they were forced to resign.

Claire Lin v Compass Group Remote Hospitality Services Pty Ltd & Anne Richardson and Another

28 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4201Employment & workplace
Ms Lin applied under s 365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), alleging she was dismissed after receiving an email about her fixed-term contract ending. The employer objected that she remained employed and had not been dismissed. The Commission upheld the jurisdictional objection and dismissed the application.
Key holding

A mistaken communication about a fixed-term contract ending does not amount to dismissal under s 386 where the employer has not terminated the employment relationship and the employee remains employed.

Noting that I am not satisfied that there was a termination of the contract of employment on 8 May 2026, further, I am not satisfied that there was a termination of the employment relationship. Ms Lin remained employed by the Respondent, and I am satisfied that she remains employed.

Ms Yan Qi v Simba Education Pty Ltd

28 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4193Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission considered an out-of-time unfair dismissal application by Ms Yan Qi against Simba Education Pty Ltd, filed five days after the 21-day statutory period. The Commission declined to extend time because it was not satisfied that exceptional circumstances existed. The unfair dismissal application was therefore dismissed.
Key holding

A conscious choice to contest a dismissal through alternative avenues and await the completion of those processes before filing an unfair dismissal application does not, of itself, amount to exceptional circumstances under s 394(3).

Taking into account the reason for the delay, namely a conscious choice to contest dismissal through alternative avenues and waiting for those processes to be complete before making the unfair dismissal application, does not amount to exceptional circumstances .

Mr Steven Kelly v P.G. Higham Pty Ltd

28 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4206Employment & workplace
This was a s.365 general protections application in which Mr Kelly alleged dismissal after presenting for work following a workers’ compensation injury. The employer denied dismissal and said he remained on its books as a casual. The Commission upheld the jurisdictional objection and dismissed the application because Mr Kelly was not dismissed.
Key holding

A refusal to permit an employee to attend work is not a dismissal under s.386 where the employee lacks medical clearance and the employer remains willing to offer work once fitness is certified.

I am not satisfied that there was a termination of the contract of employment on 22 June 2026, nor am I satisfied that there was a termination of the employment relationship. The Respondent has been prepared to consider Mr Kelly's fitness for work and offer work when he was certified fit for pre-injury duties.

Emily Lowe v Home n Heaven Pty Ltd

27 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4176Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission considered a jurisdictional objection to an unfair dismissal application by Ms Lowe against Home n Heaven Pty Ltd. The employer argued Ms Lowe had not served the minimum employment period because she had only 189 days’ service after a business purchase. The Commission found a transfer of employment occurred, so her prior service counted as continuous service.
Key holding

A probationary term in a new employment contract cannot override the statutory continuity of service arising from a transfer of employment under the Fair Work Act 2009.

The fact that the company purported to offer probationary employment to Ms Lowe does not override the provisions of the Act.

Application by Birrang Enterprise Development Co Ltd

27 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4167Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission considered Birrang’s application under s 120 of the Fair Work Act 2009 to reduce Mr Reid’s redundancy pay because it had offered him redeployment into a Support Coordinator role. Mr Reid declined the role but consented to the application. The Commission reduced his redundancy entitlement from four weeks to three weeks’ pay.
Key holding

Under s 120(1)(b)(i), whether alternative employment is acceptable is assessed objectively by the Commission, not by the employee’s subjective view, and if the preconditions are met the Commission has a broad discretion under s 120(2) to reduce redundancy pay.

Whether the alternative employment is "acceptable" is to be determined objectively, not by reference to whether Mr Reid considered that it was subjectively acceptable. The determination of whether alternative employment is acceptable requires me to make an assessment and value judgment.

Ms Diane Hamilton v EDMI Pty Ltd

27 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4187Employment & workplace
Ms Hamilton lodged a general protections dismissal application alleging adverse action based on workplace rights, disability, and temporary absence. She filed 82 days out of time and sought an extension under s 366(1) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The Fair Work Commission refused the extension and dismissed the application.
Key holding

Stress or illness associated with a dismissal does not by itself establish exceptional circumstances for an extension of time; the applicant must show the condition caused or explained the delay.

The stress that accompanies a dismissal will not, without more, favour a finding of exceptional circumstances.

Estefania Asensio Tato v Lycée Condorcet Trading AS The International French School Of Sydney Ltd

27 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4154Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission dealt with a s 739 dispute brought by a former secondary Spanish teacher against her former school over alleged underpayments/classification for February and March 2025 work. The Commission upheld the school’s jurisdictional objection because the dispute was not raised until after employment ended, dismissed the application, and noted any underpayment claim could be pursued in court. The deed of release was not determinative.
Key holding

Under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission lacks jurisdiction to determine an enterprise agreement dispute where the dispute is raised after the employment relationship has ended.

The entitlements conferred in the Agreement remain enforceable for a limited period on application to the relevant Court, but the Commission is unable to deal with the dispute under the dispute resolution clause where the dispute was raised after the employment relationship had ended.

Ms Joy Bultman v The Trustee For Scrappy's Metal Recycling Trust

27 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4149Employment & workplace
Ms Joy Bultman applied under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for an unfair dismissal remedy against The Trustee For Scrappy’s Metal Recycling Trust. She failed to attend a Commission mention/conference, did not comply with directions, filed no material by the deadline, and gave no explanation. Deputy President Bell dismissed the application for want of prosecution and no reasonable prospects of success in Bultman v The Trustee For Scrappy’s Metal Recycling Trust [2026] FWC 4149.
Key holding

Under s.587(1) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission may dismiss an application for failure to prosecute, including non-compliance with directions or failure to attend, and where no evidence means no reasonable prospects of success.

I am satisfied the power to dismiss can extend to circumstances where an applicant has failed to prosecute his or her case, including by non -compliance with directions to attend a mention/conference or file material and a repeated failure to provide a proper explanation for that non -compliance.

Application by dnata Airport Services Pty Ltd Trading AS dnata

The Fair Work Commission considered whether to approve dnata’s Queensland passenger services enterprise agreement [2026] FWC 4178. The TWU opposed approval, arguing the Agreement did not pass the better off overall test (BOOT), particularly regarding part-time shiftworker overtime and pay rates that might fall below the Award. The Commission largely accepted dnata’s Award construction and BOOT approach, but required further information or an undertaking about part-time day workers before approval.
Key holding

Ms Karen McClear v A Team Tuition Australia Pty Ltd

27 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4174Employment & workplace
Ms McClear resigned after a lengthy suspension pending an unresolved misconduct investigation and brought a s 365 general protections claim alleging she was forced to resign. A Team Tuition objected that she was not dismissed within s 386. The Commission dismissed the application, finding she was not forced to resign because of the employer’s conduct and was therefore not dismissed.
Key holding

A resignation is a dismissal under s 386(1)(b) only where an objective assessment of the employer’s conduct shows it made resignation the probable result or left the employee with no effective or real choice but to resign.

In making that assessment, it is appropriate to make an objective analysis of the Respondent's conduct to determine whether it was of such a nature that resignation was the probable result or that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign.

Ms Mariama Serray Turay v Pegasus Community Care Pty Ltd

27 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4186Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission dealt with Ms Turay’s unfair dismissal application, which was filed before the dismissal ultimately relied on took effect. The Commission found her employment was terminated on 16 September 2026 after an earlier 30 June 2026 termination notice was withdrawn by consent, so the 7 September 2026 application was premature. The Commission declined to waive the irregularity and dismissed the application.
Key holding

The Commission may decline to waive the irregularity in a premature unfair dismissal application where the applicant had a clear opportunity to withdraw and file a new application within time but did not do so.

As to whether Ms Turay could have discontinued the Application and filed a new application within time, this factor weights against waiving the irregularity.

27 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4190Employment & workplace
The AMWU applied under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Fair Work Commission to resolve a dispute over clause 17.2 of the Applus Pty Ltd Onshore NDT & Inspection Greenfields Agreement 2025. The issue was whether Easter Saturday and Easter Sunday, both falling on a weekend, entitled employees to public holidays on the next two working days or only the next working day. The Commission held each public holiday had to be taken on successive next working days.
Key holding

Under clause 17.2, where two gazetted public holidays fall on a weekend, each holiday must be taken on successive next working days so employees receive both entitlements.

Having considered the text, context and purpose, I find that the answer to the question is that employees were entitled to take the Easter Saturday public holiday on Tuesday, 7 April 2026, and the Easter Sunday public holiday on Wednesday, 8 April 2026.

"Automotive, Food, Metals, Engineering, Printing and Kindred Industries Union" known as the Australian Manufacturing Workers' Union (AMWU) (188V) v Schindler Lifts Australia Pty Ltd

26 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4166Employment & workplace
The AMWU referred a dispute under s.739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) and clause 10 of the Schindler Lifts Australia Pty Ltd Victorian Enterprise Agreement 2024–2028, asking how the "make up pay for workers comp" entitlement in clause 42 is calculated. The Commission held that "average weekly earnings" in clause 42 is to be worked out by reference to the Victorian workers' compensation concept of pre-injury average weekly earnings under the WIRC Act, and left the arithmetic to the parties.
Key holding

Where an enterprise agreement requires a top-up to 100% of "average weekly earnings" but does not define the term, that expression is to be calculated by reference to the pre-injury average weekly earnings concept in the Victorian workers' compensation legislation, with either s.153(1) or s.153(2) of the WIRC Act available.

As such, I consider that Mr Savari's 'average weekly earnings' for the purposes of clause 42 of the 2024 Agreement in relation to his workers' compensation claim for injury for the injury on 20 March 2025 are able to be calculated by reference to either s.153(1) or s.153(2) of the WIRC Act.

Application by Raquel Gray

26 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 4143Employment & workplaceContracts
The Fair Work Commission determined an unfair termination remedy application by a regulated road transport contractor, Ms Gray, against BESB Couriers after she was replaced on the Toukley delivery run upon returning from leave. The Commission found there was no valid reason for termination and that the Road Transport Industry Termination Code processes were not followed, so the termination was unfair. It ordered that a new services contract be entered into between BESB Couriers and Ms Gray personally.
Key holding

A regulated road transport contractor’s termination is unfair where there is no valid reason for termination and the processes under the Road Transport Industry Termination Code are not followed.

In summary, there was no valid reason for the termination of the services contract, and the processes in the Road Transport Code were not followed, in part because of a breakdown in communication and in part because BESB Couriers is a small business with l imited access to resources or relevant legal or human resources expertise. I am satisfied that the termination of the services contract was unfair.

The unfair dismissal application was dismissed for want of jurisdiction.
Key holding

Coverage under the Clerks—Private Sector Award 2020 requires the employee to be wholly or principally engaged in clerical work; incidental clerical duties do not establish coverage where the principal purpose of the role is management.

While I accept that some of the work performed by Mr Clay was clerical in nature, I am satisfied that he was not wholly or principally engaged in clerical work.

Under the Fair Work Act, if an unfair dismissal application has been made, it must have been withdrawn before a subsequent s 365 general protections application is made; simultaneous withdrawal in the later application does not disengage s 725.

Key holding

Key holding

Comcare v Administrative Review Tribunal

8 Oct 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 1481Migration: court challengeTribunal reviewVisa refusal reviewEmployment & workplace
Comcare sought judicial review under s 39B of the Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth) of an Administrative Review Tribunal decision refusing to release Comcare and Mr Sewell from the Harman obligation over summonsed medical records. Comcare wanted to use the records to manage Mr Sewell’s future SRC Act compensation claims after liability under s 14 was accepted by consent. The Federal Court dismissed the application, holding the Tribunal committed no jurisdictional error.
Key holding

The general functions, powers and decision-making provisions in the SRC Act do not impliedly exclude the Harman obligation for documents produced on summons in ART review proceedings concerning s 14 liability.

For these reasons, ss 69(a), 70 and 72 of the SRC Act (whether alone or in combination) do not establish a statutory inconsistency that would prevent the Harman obligation from applying to documents produced on a summons in Tribunal proceedings to determine liability under s 14 of the SRC Act.

Ms Kathleen Emery v Sharon Binding

8 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 3866Employment & workplace
Ms Emery lodged a s.365 general protections dismissal application against Ms Binding, who objected that Ms Emery was not an employee and therefore could not have been dismissed. The Fair Work Commission decided the matter on the papers and found Ms Emery was not an employee, so it dismissed the application for want of jurisdiction.
Key holding

Under s 15AA(2), employee status is determined by the totality of the relationship, including the contract terms and how the contract is performed in practice.

Section 15AA(2) requires a consideration of the totality of the relationship which involves in turn a consideration of, amongst other things, the terms of the contract between the parties and an assessment as to how the contract is performed in practice.

Mr Joshua Barbagallo v Bentrol Pty Ltd

8 Oct 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 3853Employment & workplace
Mr Barbagallo applied for an unfair dismissal remedy under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) on 10 July 2026. The Commission had to determine when his dismissal took effect and, if the application was late, whether exceptional circumstances warranted an extension. The Commission found the dismissal took effect on 10 June 2026, the application was 9 days late, and no exceptional circumstances were established, so the application was dismissed.
Key holding

Under s 394(2) and s 394(3), if an unfair dismissal application is made more than 21 days after dismissal takes effect and the Commission is not satisfied there are exceptional circumstances, it cannot allow further time and must dismiss the application.

As the application was made more than 21 days after the dismissal took effect and I am not satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances, I cannot allow Mr Barbagallo further time. I dismiss his application for an unfair dismissal remedy.

Davis and Comcare (Compensation)

25 Sep 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2403Tribunal reviewEmployment & workplace
In Davis and Comcare [2026] ARTA 2403, the Tribunal reviewed Comcare’s denial of liability for an AFP officer’s psychological injury. It found compensable PTSD caused by operational trauma between 2017 and 2021, but excluded a later aggravation of that PTSD caused by disciplinary action because it resulted from reasonable administrative action taken reasonably.
Key holding

An aggravation of a compensable mental injury is not compensable where it results from reasonable administrative action taken in a reasonable manner in respect of the employee’s employment.

Comcare is not liable to pay compensation pursuant to section 14 of the SRC Act in respect of the injury identified as aggravation of post-traumatic stress disorder being the aggravation of the existing injury also subject of the claim dated 23 May 2023 but which was the result of reasonable administrative action taken in a reasonable manner in respect of his employment with the AFP.

Key holding

Under s 218A of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission may vary an enterprise agreement to correct an obvious error, defect or irregularity, but this slip-rule power is exercised cautiously and only for uncontroversial matters.

Lifehouse Australia as the Trustee for Lifehouse Australia Trust Trading AS Chris O'Brien Lifehouse

16 Sep 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWCA 2522Employment & workplace
In Lifehouse Australia as the Trustee for Lifehouse Australia Trust Trading AS Chris O’Brien Lifehouse [2026] FWCA 2522, the employer applied under s.185 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for approval of the Chris O’Brien Lifehouse Medical Physicists Agreement 2026. The Commission noted the agreement’s annual leave and shiftworker provisions were more restrictive than the Health Professionals and Support Services Award 2020, but accepted s.190 undertakings and was satisfied the agreement passed the better off overall test.
Key holding

An enterprise agreement may pass the better off overall test despite terms more restrictive than the award where the employer demonstrates significant enhancements against the award and NES such that employees are better off overall.

The Employer provided submissions that the Agreement still passes the better off overall test because the Agreement provides for significant enhancements on the Award and the National Employment Standards (NES). I am satisfied having regard to those submissions that employees covered by the Agreement are better off overall compared to the Award.

Slowey and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security)

16 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2448Tribunal reviewVisa nominationEmployment & workplace
Mrs Slowey sought review of a Centrelink decision raising a family tax benefit debt of $1,607.51 and an interest charge of $5.02 after her adjusted taxable income included employer-provided accommodation treated as reportable fringe benefits. The Administrative Review Tribunal found the debt was due but waived it in full under s 101, and held the interest charge not payable under s 78E.
Key holding

Where an FTB debt did not arise from knowing non-compliance and there are special circumstances, beyond financial hardship alone, making waiver desirable and more appropriate than write-off, the Tribunal may waive the debt under s 101.

As it is not more appropriate to write off the debt than to waive it, the Tribunal concludes that all elements of the waiver under section 101 of the Family Assistance Administration Act are made out. The Tribunal considers that it is appropriate to waive Mrs Slowey's debt in its entirety.

Rodham and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security)

16 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2346Tribunal reviewVisa cancellationVisa nominationEmployment & workplace
Mr Rodham's jobseeker payment was cancelled after he failed to enter a Job Plan (employment pathway plan) by 22 July 2025, notwithstanding that he had lodged a Centrelink medical certificate on 24 June 2025 certifying incapacity until 24 September 2025. Centrelink did not record the temporary incapacity exemption until 19 July 2025 and conceded it could locate no record of having told him he had to enter a Job Plan within 28 days. The Tribunal set aside the cancellation and substituted a decision that payment remained payable.
Key holding

Where a claimant holds a medical certificate exempting them from mutual obligation requirements for the relevant period, and Centrelink's delay in recording that exemption (combined with a failure to notify the plan requirement) puts compliance beyond the claimant's control, the claimant is not required to satisfy the employment pathway plan requirements and payment remains payable.

The Tribunal is satisfied that these are circumstances which are beyond the person's control which made it unreasonable to expect Mr Rodham to comply with the employment pathway plan requirements in accordance with subsection 40L(2) of the Administration Act, such that a determination is in effect that Mr Rodham was not required to satisfy the employment pathway requirements for the period 24 June 2025 to 24 September 2025.

Kirby and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social Security)

16 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2292Tribunal reviewVisa nominationEmployment & workplace
The Tribunal reviewed a Centrelink decision raising a $4,109.18 newstart allowance debt against Mr Kirby for 30 November 2018 to 1 April 2019 due to undeclared employment income. The Tribunal set aside the decision and remitted the matter because Centrelink’s earlier income apportionment was not the method required under s 1117D(9) of the Social Security Act 1991. Any recalculated overpayment remains a Commonwealth debt and recovery was not waived.
Key holding

Where pre-7 December 2020 Division 3 work income is reviewed and neither the entitlement period in which it was earned nor the payroll period can be identified, it must be assessed under s 1117D(9) in the entitlement period in which it was received.

This means that the third approach in subsection 1117D(9) must be used so that [Mr Kirby's] wages are to be assessed on each day of the newstart allowance entitlement period in which he received the income.

Aldredge and Secretary, Department of Social Services (Social security)

8 Jul 2026Administrative Review Tribunal[2026] ARTA 2446Tribunal reviewEmployment & workplace
The Tribunal affirmed cancellation of Mr Aldredge’s carer payment for his son with cerebral palsy. Although the Tribunal accepted the son required substantial daily assistance from his father, the ACL questionnaire score was 54, below the statutory threshold of 85, so no qualifying rating of intense was achieved.
Key holding

A child does not achieve the qualifying rating of intense, and carer payment is not payable, where the ACL questionnaire score is less than 85.

As the score for the ACL questionnaire is less than 85 [the child] does not achieve a qualifying rating of intense and carer payment is not payable.

Mrs Narelle Wild v Hireup Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1584 (1 May 2026)

1 May 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1584Employment & workplace
This is a Fair Work Commission general protections dismissal application under s.365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Mrs Wild lodged her application 4 days after the 21-day limit and sought an extension under s.366(2). The Commission found no exceptional circumstances and dismissed the application.
Key holding

The Commission may extend time for a s.365 general protections dismissal application only if satisfied that exceptional circumstances exist under s.366(2).

Under s.366 of the FW Act, the Commission has the discretion grant an extension of time for the making of a general protections application involving dismissal. The Commission's discretion is only enlivened if it is satisfied that there are exceptional circumstances.

Ms Nicole Kinross v The Trustee For Spotlight Stores Trading Trust [2026] FWC 1381 (23 April 2026)

23 Apr 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1381Employment & workplace
Ms Nicole Kinross made an unfair dismissal application under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) against The Trustee For Spotlight Stores Trading Trust. The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application on its own initiative under s.587(1)(c) because Ms Kinross had less than six months’ employment and did not respond to Commission correspondence about the minimum employment period.
Key holding

An applicant must have completed the minimum employment period before dismissal to be eligible to make an unfair dismissal application.

A person is only eligible to make an unfair dismissal application if they have completed a minimum period of employment before their dismissal.

Paulsen v City of Hobart [2026] FCA 462 (17 April 2026)

17 Apr 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 462Employment & workplace
The Federal Court granted a self-represented applicant an extension of time under s 370(a)(ii) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) to bring a general protections claim against the City of Hobart. The originating application was filed seven days late after her prompt filing attempts were rejected by the Registry for formal deficiencies. Horan J found the delay adequately explained and extended time to 30 September 2025.
Key holding

An extension under s 370(a)(ii) does not require special circumstances, but the applicant must positively satisfy the Court that the prescribed period should be extended; prima facie the time limit applies unless there is an acceptable explanation making an extension equitable.

(1) Special circumstances are not necessary, but the Court must be positively satisfied that the prescribed period should be extended. The prima facie position is that the time limit should be complied with unless there is an acceptable explanation of the delay which makes it equitable to so extend.

Ms Ashleigh Llewellyn v Sexyland Australia Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1302 (17 April 2026)

17 Apr 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1302Employment & workplace
Ms Llewellyn made an unfair dismissal application on 27 August 2025 and then a general protections dismissal application on 2 September 2025. The Commission found the later general protections application was barred by s.725 because the earlier unfair dismissal application had not been withdrawn or failed on specified grounds, and dismissed it under s.587(1)(a).
Key holding

Section 725 prevents an applicant from making a general protections dismissal application while a prior unfair dismissal application in relation to the dismissal remains on foot, and such later application may be dismissed under s.587(1)(a).

As at 2 September 2025 when the general protections application was made, Ms Llewellyn's unfair dismissal application had not been withdrawn, failed for want of jurisdiction, or failed because the Commission found the dismissal to be a genuine redundancy. Ms Llewellyn was, therefore, prevented by section 725 from making a general protections involving dismissal application.

Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union v Qube Ports Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1331 (17 April 2026)

17 Apr 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1331Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission dealt with a s.739 dispute between the CFMEU and Qube Ports about whether the Stevedoring Industry Award 2020 prevented Qube from rostering employees who had worked a night shift to an evening shift the next calendar day. Deputy President Dean found the Agreement and Award were inconsistent on shift definitions and minimum breaks, so the Qube Ports Port of Port Kembla Enterprise Agreement 2024 prevailed. The answer to the disputed question was no.
Key holding

Where an enterprise agreement comprehensively regulates shift classifications and minimum breaks and specifically permits rostering that the Award prohibits, the inconsistency is resolved in favour of the Agreement.

The inconsistency is clear, that is the Agreement specifically allows for a rostering arrangement that the Award does not. In those circumstances, the Agreement prevails.

16 Apr 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1315Employment & workplace
Emerson Jing Wang was dismissed by Service Stream on 15 December 2025 after his RF/EME Engineer role was made redundant in a restructure. He brought an unfair dismissal application under s 394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), but the Commission upheld Service Stream’s jurisdictional objection that the dismissal was a genuine redundancy under s 389. The application was dismissed.
Key holding

A dismissal is a genuine redundancy under s 389, and cannot be an unfair dismissal under s 385, where the employer no longer requires the job to be performed by anyone due to operational changes, consultation obligations are met, and redeployment would not have been reasonable.

Given my findings above, Mr Wang's dismissal was a case of "genuine redundancy" as defined in s.389 of the FW Act. That means Mr Wang cannot satisfy the definition of an unfair dismissal in s.385 of the FW Act.

The Commission’s power to dismiss under s.587 extends beyond the enumerated grounds to cases of failure to prosecute, including non-compliance with directions and unexplained failure to provide a proper explanation.

Key holding

An unfair dismissal application cannot succeed unless the applicant has completed the minimum employment period under ss.382 and 383, and a clearly ineligible claim may be dismissed under s.587 for having no reasonable prospects.

Key holding

Under s.426(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), “significant harm” to a third party means harm above and beyond the loss, inconvenience or delay commonly caused by industrial action, not merely substantial harm.

When regard is had to context of the FW Act as a whole and to the explanatory memorandum, the expression "significant harm" in s.426(3) should be construed as having a meaning that refers to harm that has an importance or is of such consequence that it is harm above and beyond the sort of loss, inconvenience or delay that is commonly a consequence of industrial action.

Seven applicants from Fiji, employed by labour-hire company Whales but deployed to Woodward, brought s 365 general protections applications naming Woodward only after Whales dismissed them when the labour services agreement ended. Key holding

Under s 365(b) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission can only deal with a general protections dispute if the applicant actually alleges that they were dismissed in contravention of Part 3-1; merely filing a Form F8 and citing Part 3-1 is insufficient.

The mere use of a form F8 application and the citation of provisions in Part 3-1 is not a sufficient basis to conclude that a person 'alleges that the person was dismissed in contravention of this Part'. There must be an actual allegation that the person was dismissed in contravention of the Part.

ASN Events Pty Ltd v Courtney Harris-Spencer & Michelle Harris-Spencer [2026] FWC 672 (30 March 2026)

30 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 672Employment & workplace
ASN Events Pty Ltd applied under s.120 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) to reduce the redundancy pay of two former finance employees by 50%, after closing its Hastings office and offering redeployment to the Melbourne CBD. The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application, finding the employer had not obtained “other acceptable employment” for either employee because of significant additional travel time, travel costs and, for one employee, childcare responsibilities.
Key holding

Under s.120, alternative employment is acceptable only if it is objectively suitable considering matters including location and travelling time; significant travel and cost disadvantages can make otherwise like-for-like employment unacceptable.

Importantly, 'acceptable' requires that the alternative employment meets a relevant objective test. The test is not whether the alternative employment is identical, but requires consideration of whether the work is of a like nature, the effect of location, pay, the hours of work, workload, job security, fringe benefits, compliance with statutory conditions, seniority and the like, and not whether the employee finds the alternative employment to be acceptable.

Bohdi Vile v WorkPac Mining Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 1054 (27 March 2026)

27 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 1054Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission arbitrated a dispute under s.306P of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) about whether Mr Vile, a labour-hire carpenter at HVO’s Hunter Valley coal mine, was covered by a regulated labour hire arrangement order. The Commission found he was covered because he would fall within the broad Mine and Process Technician classification in the HVO Agreement. It declined to make the resulting protected rate order retrospective because the parties had not notified agreement to arbitration under s.306Q.
Key holding

Under s.306Q of the FW Act, where the parties have not notified the Commission that they agree to arbitration, an arbitrated protected rate of pay order cannot apply retrospectively and can only take effect from the date it is made or a future commencement date of the regulated labour hire arrangement order.

In contrast, if the parties have not notified the Commission that they agree to the arbitration, an arbitrated protected rate of pay order can only apply from the date the order is made, or the date the relevant regulated labour hire arrangement order will come into force if that is a future date.

Gao v Macquarie Bank Limited [2026] FCA 289 (24 March 2026)

24 Mar 2026Federal Court of Australia[2026] FCA 289Employment & workplace
In Gao v Macquarie Bank Limited [2026] FCA 289, the Federal Court dealt with interlocutory strike-out and summary-dismissal applications in a discrimination/victimisation proceeding against Macquarie Bank and three individuals, plus Fair Work adverse action claims. The applicant’s AHRC complaint named only Macquarie Bank as respondent. The Court dismissed the individual respondents and struck out various paragraphs for lack of jurisdiction, with limited leave to replead.
Key holding

Under s 46PO(1) of the AHRC Act, proceedings may only be brought against a respondent to the terminated AHRC complaint; a person merely notified under s 46PF(7) as the subject of an adverse allegation is not thereby a respondent.

That the second, third and fourth respondents were persons who were subject to adverse allegations who were notified pursuant to s 46PF(7), does not render them respondents for the purposes of s 46PO(1).

Mr Mitchell Young v The Trustee For The ThoroughClean Trust [2026] FWC 964 (23 March 2026)

23 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 964Employment & workplace
Mr Young resigned after the Respondent restructured his sales role and changed his geographic and product allocations. He brought a general protections application alleging constructive dismissal. The Fair Work Commission upheld the Respondent’s jurisdictional objection, finding Mr Young was not dismissed.
Key holding

A resignation is forced under s 386(1)(b) only where the employer’s conduct objectively intended to end the employment or made termination the probable result and left no real or effective choice but to resign.

The test to be applied here is whether the employer engaged in the conduct with the intention of bringing the employment to an end or whether termination of the employment was the probably [sic] result of the employer's conduct such that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign ... the requisite employer conduct is the essential element.

Aaden Bragg v Boom Logistics Projects Pty Ltd Trading AS Boom Projects [2026] FWC 963 (23 March 2026)

23 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 963Employment & workplace
Mr Aaden Bragg made an unfair dismissal application under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) on 4 December 2025. The Commission dismissed the application because the prescribed fee had not been paid or waived, so the application was not made in accordance with the Act. Commission staff had attempted to contact Mr Bragg on 9 and 17 December 2025 by telephone, SMS and email.
Key holding

Under s.587 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), the Commission has a discretion to dismiss an unfair dismissal application that has not been made in accordance with the Act, after giving the applicant an opportunity to rectify the deficiency and show cause.

Section 587 confers a discretion on the Commission to dismiss Mr Bragg's application if it has not been made in accordance with the Act. Mr Bragg has had ample opportunity to rectify the deficiency in his application and has had ample opportunity to show why his application should not be dismissed under s.587 (see generally Bond v Carbridge Pty Ltd T/A Carbridge [2024] FWC 1302 at [15] - [16] and the cases cited therein).

Holley Vernon v Cosmetic Wellness [2026] FWC 974 (23 March 2026)

23 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 974Employment & workplace
Ms Holley Vernon made an unfair dismissal application under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) against Cosmetic Wellness. The Commission dismissed the application on its own initiative because the information showed she had not served the minimum employment period and the claim had no reasonable prospects of success.
Key holding

The Commission may dismiss an application on its own initiative under s.587 only where it is very clear there are no reasonable prospects of success and no disputed facts could affect the outcome.

An application should not be dismissed under s.587 unless it is very clear that there are no reasonable prospects of success. As such the power under s.587 is not available if there are disputed facts that could affect the outcome of the proceedings.

Silence Ko v Transit Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 947 (20 March 2026)

20 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 947Employment & workplace
Silence Ko applied for an unfair dismissal remedy after being dismissed by Transit Pty Ltd on 10 December 2025, having started on 27 October 2025. The Fair Work Commission dismissed the application on its own initiative because the Applicant could not satisfy the minimum employment period required by ss 382 and 383 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The Commission found the application had no reasonable prospects of success under s 587(1)(c).
Key holding

Subject to procedural fairness, the Commission may dismiss an unfair dismissal application on its own initiative under s 587 where it has no reasonable prospects of success because the minimum employment period cannot be satisfied.

Subject to affording procedural fairness, s 587 of the Act allows the Commission to dismiss an application on the Commission's own initiative in the early stages of proceedings. Protracted proceedings can be avoided when there is no reasonable prospect of an outcome other than the dismissal of the application.

Tanzeel Ur Rehman was deactivated from Portier Pacific Pty Ltd’s Uber Driver Platform on 15 December 2025 and applied for an unfair deactivation remedy under s 536LU of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The FWC made a formal reactivation order under s 536LQ(1) and an order for lost remuneration of $7,096.96 gross under s 536LQ(3).
Key holding

However, that a respondent to an application under s 536LU may avert the issuance of an order to restore lost pay under s 536LQ(3) of the Act by voluntarily taking measures as referred to in s 536LQ(1) and contending that an order under s 536LQ(1) is of no utility and therefore the Commission has no basis upon which to make such order, appears contrary to the legislative intent of the provision.

The Commission may dismiss an unfair dismissal application on its own initiative under s 587(1)(c) where, after procedural fairness, the application has no reasonable prospects of success.

Subject to affording procedural fairness, s 587 of the Act allows the Commission to dismiss an application on the Commission's own initiative in the early stages of proceedings. Protracted proceedings can be avoided when there is no reasonable prospect of an outcome other than the dismissal of the application.

Clause 30.5(g) requires the divisor for calculating the percentage of night shifts to be the total possible shifts the employee can actually work in the relevant roster cycle, determined by the employee’s roster pattern rather than a notional figure.

The clause requires the total possible shifts an employee can work in the relevant roster cycle to be determined based on the shifts the employee works, not a notional figure. That figure is the divisor for the calculation.

Gary Henry Mountney v H-E Parts International Mining Solutions Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 796 (11 March 2026)

11 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 796Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission dismissed Mr Mountney’s s.394 unfair dismissal application because it was filed six days late and the Commission was not satisfied there were exceptional circumstances to extend time under s.394(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). Mr Mountney relied principally on a pre-booked family holiday, but the Commission found this did not explain the whole delay.
Key holding

A pre-booked family holiday does not amount to exceptional circumstances under s.394(3) where it fails to explain the whole delay and the applicant had time before and after the holiday to lodge.

In those circumstances, the pre-booked holiday does not satisfactorily explain the entirety of the delay, nor does it demonstrate circumstances that were out of the ordinary course, or unusual, or special, or uncommon so as to be characterised as exceptional.

Jodie Daunis v Rivercity Ferries Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 740 (5 March 2026)

5 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 740Employment & workplace
Ms Daunis, a long-serving ferry customer service operator with DVT/Factor V Leiden, was dismissed by Rivercity Ferries in July 2025 after extended absences. The Fair Work Commission found the dismissal was not unfair because she could not perform the inherent duties at the time, no reasonable adjustments were practical, and procedural fairness had been afforded. The unfair dismissal application was dismissed.
Key holding

A capacity-based dismissal can be valid where the medical evidence at termination does not establish that the employee will be fit for the full inherent duties in the reasonably foreseeable future.

I am satisfied that the evidence does not support such a conclusion. I accept that while the medical evidence is inconsistent and contradictory, when considered overall as at the time of the termination it fell well short of clearly indicating Ms Daunis would be fit to return to her full duties in the foreseeable future, and instead was premised on assumptions about factors including the scheduled surgery in November 2025.

Amy Doran v The Jewellery Group Pty Limited [2026] FWC 673 (5 March 2026)

5 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 673Employment & workplace
Amy Doran alleged she was forced to resign from The Jewellery Group Pty Limited and applied to the Fair Work Commission under s 365 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The Respondent objected on jurisdiction, arguing Ms Doran was not dismissed because she resigned voluntarily. The Commission dismissed the application, finding Ms Doran had not been “dismissed” for the purposes of s 386.
Key holding

Under s 386(1)(b), a resignation is a dismissal only if the employer’s conduct left the employee no real choice but to resign, and the line between forced and voluntary resignation is narrow.

The line distinguishing conduct that leaves an employee no real choice but to resign from an employee resigning at their own initiative is a narrow one.

Joel Sweeney v Drew Stephenson Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 723 (5 March 2026)

5 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 723Employment & workplace
Joel Sweeney applied under s.394 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) alleging unfair dismissal after Drew Stephenson Pty Ltd terminated his employment as a Junior Accountant on 8 August 2025. The Commission upheld the employer’s jurisdictional objection that the dismissal was a genuine redundancy under s.389, so the unfair dismissal application was dismissed. The Commission also rejected arguments about continued trading and award coverage.
Key holding

Under s 389(1) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth), a genuine redundancy does not require the employer to prove insolvency or cessation of trading; the inquiry is whether operational changes meant the job was no longer required, without a reasonableness assessment.

As was noted by the High Court, s.389(1) is not subject to a reasonableness enquiry. All that is required is that changes in operational requirements are established.

National Tertiary Education Industry Union v The University Of Newcastle [2026] FWC 727 (4 March 2026)

The NTEU applied under s 739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) for the Fair Work Commission to arbitrate disputes with the University of Newcastle over alleged failures to consult and comply with WHS obligations regarding 2025 major workplace change. Deputy President Saunders held the Commission had a discretion to arbitrate and decided to exercise it.

Ms Xanthe Thomson, a PSA Industrial Officer, applied under s.739 of the Fair Work Act 2009 disputing the PSA’s misconduct process over alleged timesheet falsification. The Commission held the PSA breached cl 51 of the Public Service Association of NSW Staff Enterprise Agreement 2024 because the Assistant Secretary both investigated/formulated the allegations and assessed her response/recommended dismissal. In relation to clause 6 of the Policy as extracted at paragraph [23] of this decision, put simply, the Respondent has conflated two of the steps in the process by having the Assistant Secretary act as the Applicant's manager and also act as the independent investigator. As a result, the process lacks the required procedural fairness, so the application must succeed.

Cameron Lewien v Triple Zero Victoria [2026] FWC 722 (4 March 2026)

4 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 722Employment & workplace
Cameron Lewien was dismissed by Triple Zero Victoria after Victoria Police revoked his security clearance and refused to reinstate it, leaving him unable to access Victoria Police information required for his Data Group Lead role. Key holding

A security clearance can be an inherent requirement of a role even if it is not expressly stated in the employment contract.

It is well established that the absence of an inherent requirement being specified in a contract of employment, does not mean the relevant requirement cannot be an inherent requirement of a position.

Brent Houston v AWX Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 702 (3 March 2026)

3 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 702Employment & workplace
Brent Houston brought a s 365 general protections application against labour-hire employer AWX Pty Ltd after his placement ended and AWX issued a separation certificate citing “shortage of work”. AWX objected that the Commission lacked jurisdiction because Mr Houston had not been dismissed. Deputy President Colman found the employment ended on the employer’s initiative, dismissed the objection, and issued a s 368 certificate while indicating no reasonable prospect of success under s 369 or in court.
Key holding

Where an employer issues a separation certificate citing shortage of work and does not confirm or record that a casual employee is resigning, the employment is treated as terminated on the employer’s initiative and the employee is dismissed under s 386(1)(a).

But if AWX believes the casual is resigning, it should confirm this and also state in the certificate that the employee is ceasing work voluntarily. In my view Mr Houston's employment was terminated on the employer's initiative, and he was therefore dismissed within the meaning of s 386(1)(a) of the Act.

Kellie Fitzpatrick v University of New South Wales [2026] FWC 677 (2 March 2026)

2 Mar 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 677Employment & workplace
Ms Kellie Fitzpatrick referred a dispute to the Fair Work Commission under s.65B(3) of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth) after UNSW did not accept her request to change her existing hybrid part-time arrangement to work exclusively from home for three days each week. The Commission found the request was not made “because of” her eligible parent circumstance and dismissed the application. UNSW therefore had no responsive obligations under s.65A.
Key holding

Under s.65, a request for flexible working arrangements is validly made only if there is a causal connection between the employee’s eligible circumstance and the requested change.

For these reasons, I find no causal connection between the circumstance of Ms Fitzpatrick as a parent of a young child and her request to work full time from home, whether for a finite or indefinite period, to support a move interstate. The request made on 3 September 2025 was not validly made under s.65 of the Act.

The Fair Work Commission found that Mr Houstein, a truck driver, was dismissed rather than having genuinely resigned after a heated exchange with a leading hand on 17 June 2025. The matter will now proceed to a merits hearing.
Key holding

An ostensible resignation made in the heat of the moment and not genuinely intended, where the employer ought to appreciate that, is a dismissal at the employer’s initiative under s 386.

In all the circumstances, I consider that Mr Houstein's resignation was made in the heat of the moment, was not genuine, and that the employer ought to have appreciated this. The termination of the employment must therefore be taken to be at the employer's initiative, and is a dismissal for the purposes of section 386 of the Act.

The CFMEU applied under s.437 of the Fair Work Act 2009 for a protected action ballot order covering employees of Etex Australia Pty Ltd. Key holding

On a s.437 application, the Commission need not refuse a protected action ballot order merely because ballot questions are ambiguous or lack clarity; the questions need only describe the proposed industrial action so employees are capable of responding, with ambiguity potentially affecting later protection.

If the questions are ambiguous or lack clarity there may be consequences for the bargaining representative and the employees if reliance is placed on the result of the ballot in taking industrial action.

Key holding

A declaration of results showing employee voting proportions is relevant information for good faith bargaining and may need to be disclosed absent confidentiality or commercial sensitivity, because it can inform whether bargaining positions should change and help avoid protracted bargaining.

What proportion of employees vote in favour of an agreement is critically relevant to bargaining. At either end of the extreme, and to varying degrees in between, whether none agree or 49% agree is crucial information in terms of whether the proposed terms and conditions are satisfactory to the majority of the workforce, or whether either side should give consideration to modifying their bargaining position to avoid protracted bargaining.

Naomi Harnett v Hands On People Pty Ltd [2026] FWC 636 (26 February 2026)

26 Feb 2026Fair Work Commission[2026] FWC 636Employment & workplace
The Fair Work Commission considered a jurisdictional objection to a s.365 general protections application brought by a former HR manager who alleged she was constructively dismissed. The Commission upheld the objection, finding the Applicant had not been dismissed within s.386 of the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth). The decision turned on whether the Employer’s conduct forced her resignation.
Key holding

For a s.386(1)(b) forced-resignation dismissal, the employer’s conduct must be intended to bring employment to an end, or be of such a nature that termination was the probable result and the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign.

A resignation that is "forced" by conduct or a course of conduct on the part of the employer will be a dismissal within the second limb of the definition in s.386(1)(b). The test to be applied here is whether the employer engaged in the conduct with the intention of bringing the employment to an end or whether termination of the employment was the probably result of the employer's conduct such that the employee had no effective or real choice but to resign.

Key holding

A ban on complying with an employer policy or work requirement is industrial action only if it causes work to be performed differently and results in a restriction, limitation or delay on normal work, or itself restricts or limits work.

Mr Matthew Duncan Hatch v Woodside Energy Ltd.

23 Jan 2026Fair Work Commission (Full Bench)[2023] FWCFB 51Employment & workplace
Mr Hatch lodged a general protections dismissal application against Woodside Energy. Deputy President Young found it was one day out of time and refused an extension. On appeal the Full Bench held the application was in fact lodged within the 21-day period because, applying the Acts Interpretation Act and state time rules, it was received by 11:59 pm Perth time on the final day. The appeal was upheld, the decision quashed, and the matter remitted for conciliation.

Jae Challis signed a contractor agreement with Meta Healthcare to provide disability support services, but the Commission found he was in fact a casual employee. Meta's jurisdictional objection was upheld and the general protections application was dismissed.

Kylie Wykes was dismissed by Wilmar Sugar after leaving her station early and prior sleeping-on-the-job reports. Leigh v State of Queensland
